n: Naaman is Aram’s top general—respected, victorious, and brave. Surprisingly, the text credits his victories to the Lord, the God of Israel, who rules all nations. Yet he has a skin disease that no rank can cure.

f.g: Hebrew tsara’at covered various serious skin diseases, not only modern leprosy (Hansen’s disease).

n: Aramean raiders had captured a young Israelite girl, who now serves Naaman’s wife. She has lost home and family.
Rather than bitterness, the girl shows compassion and faith: she wishes her master could meet the prophet in Samaria, who could heal him. One small, faithful voice starts the whole story.
Naaman reports her words to the king of Aram.
The king sends Naaman with a letter and a fortune in gifts—about 750 pounds of silver, 150 pounds of gold, and ten sets of fine clothing. He assumes healing can be bought.
The letter asks Israel’s king to cure Naaman, as though the king controlled the prophet.
Israel’s king (probably Jehoram) panics and tears his robes: only God can give life or death. He assumes Aram is looking for an excuse for war. He does not even think of Elisha.

f.w: Am I God, to kill and to make alive

n: Elisha sends word: “Send him to me, and he will know there is a prophet in Israel.”
Naaman arrives in grand style with horses and chariots and waits at Elisha’s door.
Elisha doesn’t even come out. He sends a messenger: wash seven times in the Jordan, and you will be clean. The simplicity is a test of humility.
Naaman is furious. He expected a dramatic ceremony with the prophet waving his hand over the diseased spot.

f.w: strike his hand over the place
f.g: wave his hand over the affected area.

n: Damascus had clear rivers fed by mountain springs; the Jordan was muddy by comparison. Naaman storms off in pride.

f.g: rivers flowing through and near Damascus.

n: His servants reason with him gently: If the prophet had asked something hard, you would have done it. Why not something this easy? Often the Lord’s simple commands are the hardest for the proud to obey.

f.w: if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing

n: Naaman humbles himself, dips seven times, and his skin becomes like a little child’s. Many see in this a picture of baptism and spiritual rebirth.

f.w: the flesh of a little child

n: Naaman returns to confess: there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. He offers Elisha a gift.
Elisha firmly refuses payment. God’s gifts are not for sale, and Naaman must know his healing came from God, not a purchase.
Naaman asks for two mule-loads of Israel’s soil to take home, so he can worship the Lord on Israelite earth. He vows to worship no other god.

f.g: many ancients believed a god was tied to his land; Naaman wanted to worship on Israel’s soil.

n: He asks pardon in advance: his duty will require him to support his king as he bows in the temple of Rimmon, Aram’s storm god. His conscience is now sensitive.

f.g: ‘thunderer,’ a title of the Aramean storm-god Hadad.
Naaman was the king’s attendant officer.

n: Elisha simply says, “Go in peace,” leaving the matter between Naaman and God.

f.g: Hebrew lekh leshalom, a blessing of peace.

n: Gehazi thinks his master was foolish to let this rich foreigner go without paying. He swears he will get something—greed taking the Lord’s name in vain.
Naaman, now humble, steps down from his chariot to greet the servant—an act of respect.
Gehazi lies, inventing a story about two visiting young prophets in need.
Naaman generously gives double and has servants carry it.
At “the tower” (the hill, or citadel) Gehazi takes the goods, hides them in the house, and dismisses the servants.

f.g: Hebrew ophel: a hill or fortified mound.

n: Elisha asks where he has been. Gehazi lies again: “Nowhere.”
Elisha says his spirit was with Gehazi and saw it all. Is this the time to take money—when a foreigner has just learned that God’s grace is free?

f.w: Went not mine heart with thee

n: Gehazi receives Naaman’s leprosy. The foreigner who humbled himself went home clean; the Israelite servant who grasped for wealth went out unclean. The story invites every reader to choose humility over greed.
